title: Understanding the menstrual cycle
intro: The menstrual cycle links hormone signals, ovarian activity and changes in the uterine lining. Timing varies between people and across life. A textbook pattern or calendar app cannot reliably prove ovulation or exclude pregnancy.

sections.heading: Starting a cycle
paragraphs: The first day of menstrual bleeding marks a new cycle. Brain and pituitary signals stimulate follicles in the ovaries; estrogen helps rebuild the uterine lining.

sections.heading: Ovulation
paragraphs: A hormone surge can trigger release of an egg into a fallopian tube. Ovulation does not occur on an identical calendar day for everyone, and bleeding does not guarantee that it occurred.

sections.heading: After release
paragraphs: The emptied follicle forms a temporary structure that produces progesterone. This supports the lining; if pregnancy does not develop, hormone levels fall and the lining sheds.

sections.heading: Everyday tracking
paragraphs: Record bleeding, pain and effects on daily life without treating every variation as disease. Puberty, menopause transition, illness, stress and hormonal contraception can alter patterns; calendar counting alone is unreliable contraception.

sections.heading: Seeking care
paragraphs: Very heavy bleeding, faintness, severe pain, persistent irregularity or bleeding after menopause needs assessment. Possible pregnancy with severe one-sided pain, collapse or shoulder-tip pain needs urgent care even before a positive home test.

A diagram explains typical structure, not the cause of an individual symptom. Before a consultation, note when a change began, what brings it on and how it affects daily activities. Bring previous results and ask how the findings fit together.
